text: This mouthwash was sold to scrub floors.
Surgeons used it on wounds. Janitors used it on floors.
As a mouthwash? Barely anyone cared.
Around 1921, Gerard Lambert, the boss's son, needed people to want it.
His team dug up an old medical word: halitosis.
Bad breath wasn't a smell anymore. It was a condition. And your friends would never tell you.
Then came Edna. Often a bridesmaid, never a bride.
Her problem? Not her looks. Her breath.
In seven years, revenue reportedly jumped from $115,000 to over $8 million.
They didn't sell a cure. They sold the fear.
